question_en: Which option best describes your professional role?
option_1_en: Radiation oncologist
option_2_en: Medical physicist
option_3_en: Radiation therapist
option_4_en: Other, including dosimetrist or researcher

question_en: Which stage best describes your professional career? Count years from when you qualified to practise independently in your profession (for doctors, completion of specialist training).
option_1_en: In training, or less than 5 years since qualifying to practise independently
option_2_en: 5 to less than 10 years since qualifying to practise independently
option_3_en: 10 to less than 20 years since qualifying to practise independently
option_4_en: 20 or more years since qualifying to practise independently

question_en: Which category occupies the largest share of your working time? Select mixed or other if no listed category predominates.
option_1_en: Clinical practice
option_2_en: Research
option_3_en: Management or education
option_4_en: Mixed role or other responsibilities

question_en: What is the most formal type of AI or machine-learning education you have completed?
option_1_en: Assessed learning, such as a degree module or assessed course
option_2_en: Unassessed courses, workshops or seminars
option_3_en: Self-directed learning only
option_4_en: No AI education or training

question_en: How would you rate your understanding of the strengths and limitations of clinical AI? Select the description that best fits your current knowledge.
option_1_en: Minimal: I am unfamiliar with the main strengths and limitations of clinical AI.
option_2_en: Basic: I recognise common terms but struggle to explain their practical implications.
option_3_en: Intermediate: I can explain common limitations and apply them to familiar clinical examples.
option_4_en: Advanced: I can critically assess evidence, assumptions and limitations in unfamiliar clinical examples.

question_en: How comfortable are you using AI terminology accurately, such as machine learning, U-Net, large language models and calibration?
option_1_en: Not at all comfortable
option_2_en: Somewhat comfortable
option_3_en: Quite comfortable
option_4_en: Very comfortable

question_en: How important is understanding AI concepts for your current job role?
option_1_en: Not at all important
option_2_en: Slightly important
option_3_en: Moderately important
option_4_en: Very important

question_en: Which statement best describes the relationship between AI and machine learning?
option_1_en: AI learns from labelled examples, whereas machine learning learns from unlabelled examples.
option_2_en: AI uses neural networks, whereas machine learning uses manually programmed decision rules.
option_3_en: AI is the broader field, whereas machine learning is the subset of AI that learns from data.
option_4_en: AI produces recommendations, whereas machine learning only describes patterns in existing data.
explanation_en: Machine learning is a subset of AI in which models learn patterns from data. AI also includes approaches based on explicitly programmed rules, so a system described as AI need not use machine learning. Neural networks are one family of machine-learning models, and machine learning is used for prediction as well as description.
help_terms_en: Neural network: A type of model built from many connected layers of simple mathematical units. | Decision rule: An explicit if-then instruction written by a person, for example 'flag the plan if cord maximum dose exceeds tolerance'.
clinical_context_en: Many radiotherapy products are now marketed as using 'AI', and vendor descriptions of how they work vary widely.

question_en: An AI contouring tool was developed using supervised learning. What does this describe?
option_1_en: Clinicians supervise the model every time it processes a new patient's scan.
option_2_en: Clinicians validate the model's predictions after its training has been completed.
option_3_en: The model groups unlabelled scans according to shared anatomical image features.
option_4_en: The model learns from scans paired with reference contours during training.
explanation_en: Supervised learning uses paired inputs and reference outputs during training, such as CT scans and reference contours. This describes the learning process, not clinical supervision during use or independent validation after development.
clinical_context_en: Most commercial auto-contouring tools are described as using supervised learning, and the term appears throughout vendor documents and papers.

question_en: Staff have edited an AI contouring model's outputs for two years, and a colleague asks if it has now learned the department's contouring style? Which statement about its model parameters is correct?
option_1_en: They gradually adapt to the average shape of the locally approved contours.
option_2_en: They stay the same, changing only if a separate training or model-update process is run.
option_3_en: They are adjusted when edited contours are saved to the connected planning database.
option_4_en: They may adapt slowly, so changes would be hard to notice without a formal audit.
explanation_en: A locked model's parameters do not change through routine use, so two years of edits have not altered it. Local adaptation requires a separate training or update process, and any resulting model change needs version control, validation and change management.
help_terms_en: Model parameters: The internal numerical values a model uses to turn an input, such as a CT scan, into an output, such as a contour. Also called weights.
clinical_context_en: Auto-contouring tools often remain in use for years while staff correct their output every day. Whether those corrections change the tool affects what reviewers should expect from it.

question_en: The internal decision process of an AI contouring model is difficult to interpret. What does this imply for evaluating its clinical performance?
option_1_en: Independent test data and clinical review still allow its clinical performance to be evaluated locally.
option_2_en: Access to every model weight is needed before an independent performance evaluation can be meaningful.
option_3_en: A saliency map that highlights the anatomy considered by the model indicates whether the contour can be trusted clinically.
option_4_en: When internal processes are inaccessible, the vendor's published performance is the best available evidence.
explanation_en: Limited interpretability does not prevent independent performance evaluation, clinical review or ongoing monitoring, and vendor results do not replace local evaluation. Saliency and attention visualisations may provide additional information, but they do not establish clinical correctness and may not faithfully explain the prediction.
help_terms_en: Saliency map: A heatmap overlaid on the image showing which regions most influenced the model's output. | Model weight: One of the internal numerical values set during model development.
clinical_context_en: Most deep-learning contouring and planning tools cannot explain why they drew a particular boundary, yet departments must still decide whether and how to use them.

question_en: A vendor describes a new AI system as a foundation model. Which feature best supports that description?
option_1_en: It has far more parameters than conventional models built for a single clinical task.
option_2_en: It learns the local clinical task by updating its parameters after each approved output.
option_3_en: It is broadly pretrained to support adaptation to a range of downstream tasks.
option_4_en: It combines several separately trained task-specific tools without sharing a pretrained model.
explanation_en: Foundation models learn reusable representations through broad pretraining and can be adapted to multiple downstream tasks. Large size, multiple tools or continuous updating alone do not define a foundation model. Each proposed clinical use still needs suitable task-specific and local evaluation.
help_terms_en: Parameters: The internal numerical values set during model development.
clinical_context_en: Vendors increasingly market 'foundation models' for imaging, contouring and report writing.

question_en: An AI contouring model performed well at its development centre. Which statement best describes its transferability to your department?
option_1_en: Performance may differ here, because scanners, populations and contouring conventions affect it.
option_2_en: When the imaging modality matches, acquisition-protocol differences are unlikely to affect performance.
option_3_en: Local contouring conventions matter less when both departments use the same planning software.
option_4_en: It cannot be used safely at a new site until it has been retrained on local patient data.
explanation_en: Sites may differ in scanners, reconstruction, contrast use, patient populations and reference-contouring conventions. These differences can affect model performance even when the imaging modality and planning software are the same. Local evaluation is needed to assess transferability; retraining is not automatically required.
help_terms_en: Imaging modality: The type of imaging, such as CT, MRI or PET. | Acquisition protocol: The scanner settings used to capture images, such as slice thickness, tube voltage or contrast timing.
clinical_context_en: Many commercial AI tools are developed using data from a small number of centres and then sold to departments across Europe and beyond.

question_en: A report evaluates AI contours against clinician-drawn 'ground truth'. Which interpretation of the ground truth is most appropriate?
option_1_en: Clinician-drawn contours are unsuitable for evaluation because clinicians disagree on boundaries.
option_2_en: Clinican drawn contours reflect annotation conventions and observer variability, not error-free truth.
option_3_en: Consensus contours remove the uncertainty at poorly visible boundaries, so they can be treated as exact.
option_4_en: Agreement with a ground-truth contour directly measures the biological accuracy of a tumour boundary.
explanation_en: Clinician-defined contours are useful reference standards, but they can contain uncertainty, disagreement and annotation errors. Consensus can improve consistency without eliminating uncertainty. Agreement with these labels should not be equated with perfect anatomical or biological accuracy.
help_terms_en: Consensus contour: A single reference contour agreed by several clinicians, for example through joint review or by combining their individual contours.
clinical_context_en: AI contouring papers and vendor reports commonly present their results as agreement with 'ground truth'.

question_en: An AI model was trained on over one million medical images. What does this imply about the possibility of clinically harmful bias?
option_1_en: A large enough image count compensates for a narrow range of patient populations or sites.
option_2_en: Bias is unavoidable at this scale, so the outputs cannot be relied on for any patient subgroup.
option_3_en: Bias concerns apply mainly to small datasets, so subgroup analysis is not needed at this scale.
option_4_en: Dataset size alone does not guarantee representative patients or unbiased, consistent labels.
explanation_en: Size alone does not establish representativeness or label quality. Bias can arise from sampling, measurement, annotation and modelling choices, and strong aggregate performance can conceal poorer performance in relevant subgroups, so subgroup analysis remains necessary however large the dataset. Bias is not inevitable or unmeasurable: subgroup evaluation can show where performance is acceptable.
help_terms_en: Subgroup analysis: Reporting performance separately for groups of patients, for example by sex, disease site or scanner type.
clinical_context_en: Vendors often cite very large training datasets, sometimes millions of images, as a selling point for their products.

question_en: Your department changes its CT reconstruction protocol. Which interpretation of is most appropriate?
option_1_en: Because the model version is unchanged, its validated performance can be assumed to carry over.
option_2_en: Any reconstruction change invalidates the model, so it should be retrained on the new images.
option_3_en: This primarily changes image appearance, so the original contour validation remains applicable.
option_4_en: Image characteristics may change enough to affect contour quality without any software error.
explanation_en: A reconstruction change may alter image characteristics such as noise and texture, introducing a shift in model inputs. Successful software execution does not establish unchanged clinical performance, but retraining is not automatically required. Assess the change and perform proportionate, targeted revalidation where needed.
help_terms_en: Reconstruction protocol: The settings used to turn raw CT scanner measurements into images, such as kernel, iterative reconstruction strength and slice thickness.
clinical_context_en: CT protocols change from time to time, for example for dose reduction, scanner replacement or new reconstruction software.

question_en: A pelvic planning scan contains bilateral hip prostheses and extensive postoperative reconstruction. Which statement about the AI contouring tool's reliability is most appropriate?
option_1_en: Its output is unusable for this patient, because AI contours fail whenever metal implants are present.
option_2_en: Its routine-case accuracy is likely to be a reasonable guide to its reliability for this patient.
option_3_en: These features may be rare in the development data, raising the risk of errors that look plausible.
option_4_en: Atypical cases can be assessed using the model's confidence score without checking its validated scope.
explanation_en: Unusual anatomy and artefacts may be poorly represented during development or outside the validated scope. A model can produce plausible-looking contours despite clinically important errors, but metal implants do not automatically make the output unusable. Check intended use and relevant validation evidence, and review the output carefully; rarity alone does not formally establish that a case is out-of-distribution.
help_terms_en: Validated scope: The patients, anatomy and imaging conditions in which a tool's performance has been tested and documented. | Development data: The images used to build and tune a model. | Confidence score: A number some tools display alongside an output to indicate how certain the model is.
clinical_context_en: Hip prostheses cause metal streak artefacts on planning CT, and pelvic surgery can move organs from their usual positions. These patients still need their organs at risk contoured for planning.

question_en: A locked model predicts 2-year mortality in patients receiving radiotherapy. It was trained before an effective systemic treatment became standard care. How could this affect its predictions?
option_1_en: The model becomes unreliable only if the definitions of its recorded input variables change.
option_2_en: Its ability to rank patients by risk is necessarily lost once standard care changes.
option_3_en: Calibration is likely to hold, because the recorded baseline features have similar distributions.
option_4_en: The relationship between baseline features and mortality may change, affecting calibration.
explanation_en: Concept shift is a change in the relationship between predictors and outcomes. An effective treatment absent from model development can alter mortality for otherwise similar patients, potentially causing overprediction of risk. Ranking may be partly preserved even while calibration drifts. Monitor predicted and observed outcomes rather than relying only on stable input distributions.
help_terms_en: Systemic treatment: Drug treatment that acts throughout the body, such as chemotherapy or immunotherapy. | Baseline features: Patient characteristics recorded before treatment, such as age, stage and performance status.
clinical_context_en: Outcome models are often developed on patients treated several years earlier, and standard care can evolve in that time, as with consolidation immunotherapy after chemoradiotherapy for stage III lung cancer.

question_en: A vendor uses the same patient scans to select model hyperparameters (e.g guide model design) and to report final test performance. Which statement about the reported performance is most accurate?
option_1_en: The test scans influenced model selection, so the reported estimate is not independent.
option_2_en: Averaging accuracy over repeated tuning runs can correct for reusing the same scans.
option_3_en: Reusing the scans can be acceptable if the final model weights are frozen before reporting.
option_4_en: The model should be discarded, because tuning on these scans means it cannot generalise.
explanation_en: Hyperparameters: Settings chosen by developers rather than learned from the data, such as network size or how long to train.
help_terms_en: Vendor and published performance figures are often the main evidence available when procuring an AI tool for radiotherapy.

question_en: During further training, a segmentation model's training error continues to fall while its error on independent validation patients begins to rise. Both datasets represent comparable patients, imaging protocols and contouring guidance. Which explanation is most consistent with this pattern?
option_1_en: Underfitting, with insufficient capacity to capture useful patterns in either dataset.
option_2_en: Distribution shift, with the validation patients differing systematically from the training patients.
option_3_en: Data leakage, with information from the validation patients also appearing in the training data.
option_4_en: Overfitting, with additional training improving fit to training cases but worsening generalisation.
explanation_en: This divergence is characteristic of overfitting: additional training improves fit to development cases without improving performance on unseen cases. The scenario rules out distribution shift, leakage would tend to make validation error look better rather than worse, and underfitting would show high error in both datasets. Poor performance at a different hospital alone would not establish overfitting, because distribution shift or differences in reference standards could also explain it.
help_terms_en: Training error: The model's error on the cases it is learning from.
clinical_context_en: Plots of training and validation error appear in vendor technical files and AI papers, including those for auto-contouring tools.

question_en: A small single-centre training dataset is expanded tenfold using rotations and synthetic noise. What can reasonably be concluded about this augmentation?
option_1_en: The tenfold increase provides nearly as much information as collecting ten times more patients.
option_2_en: It targets robustness to the simulated variations, not representativeness of new populations.
option_3_en: Synthetic images add no useful information, because they are derived from the same patients.
option_4_en: Performance on transformed training images can serve as a test of transportability to other hospitals.
explanation_en: Appropriate transformations can improve robustness to the variations they simulate, so augmentation does add useful information. It does not create equivalent numbers of independent patients, correct biased labels or establish performance in unrepresented populations. Use clinically plausible transformations and evaluate generalisation with independent data.
help_terms_en: Data augmentation: Creating extra training examples by altering existing images, for example by rotating them or adding noise. | Transportability: How well a model's performance carries over to a different hospital or population.
clinical_context_en: Contoured radiotherapy data are slow and expensive to produce, so developers commonly expand small datasets artificially, particularly for less common treatment sites.

question_en: What does transfer learning mean in the context of clinical artificial intelligence (AI)?
option_1_en: Training an AI model from scratch using only data from a specific hospital or clinical setting.
option_2_en: Adapting an AI model that has already learned from one dataset or task to perform a related task.
option_3_en: It means the original training population no longer influences performance once local cases are added.
option_4_en: Using the same AI model without any changes across all patient populations and clinical settings.
explanation_en: Transfer learning can reuse useful representations from pretraining, reducing the data or computation needed for a related task. Benefits depend on task and domain compatibility. Fine-tuning can still overfit, so evaluation on independent, relevant data remains necessary.
help_terms_en: Fine-tuning: Further training of an existing model on a smaller dataset for a specific task.
clinical_context_en: Vendors and research groups commonly adapt existing models to new organs, local protocols or new centres.

question_en: An AI spinal cord contour has a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.92 against a reference contour. Which interpretation is most appropriate for planning review?
option_1_en: At this level of overlap, any remaining boundary error is likely too small to change cord dose.
option_2_en: It reports the largest boundary displacement, which must be checked against an accepted tolerance.
option_3_en: It summarises overlap, so it can conceal a local boundary error near a steep dose gradient.
option_4_en: It estimates agreement in maximum cord dose, but does not describe the location of that dose.
explanation_en: Dice measures volume overlap, not local boundary displacement or dose impact. A small local error may matter clinically while having little effect on overall overlap. Training losses based on overlap need not weight errors by clinical consequence. Use appropriate anatomical, geometric and dosimetric assessment; additional geometric metrics do not by themselves establish safety.
help_terms_en: Dmax: The highest dose received anywhere in a structure.
clinical_context_en: Auto-contour QA reports and papers commonly quote Dice scores. The spinal cord is a dose-limiting organ in head-and-neck, lung and spine SBRT planning.

question_en: A validation review finds the AI contours clinically acceptable in 470 of 500 patients. Of these 500 patients, 5/20 postoperative patients had acceptable contours. Which conclusion is best supported?
option_1_en: The model should be withdrawn for all patients because one subgroup performed poorly.
option_2_en: The subgroup's estimate can be replaced by the overall rate because its sample size is smaller.
option_3_en: Overall acceptability masks poorer postoperative performance, which warrants focused evaluation.
option_4_en: With only 20 patients, the postoperative result is too imprecise to justify further action.
explanation_en: Overall acceptability is 94% (470/500), compared with 25% (5/20) in postoperative cases and approximately 95% (460/480) in the other remaining cases. The postoperative estimate is imprecise (for example it's 95% confidence interval being roughly 30-70%), but even this upper bound is well below the rate in other patients, so the difference warrants investigation rather than dismissal or withdrawal for all patients. Report subgroup sample sizes and uncertainty, and assess suitability by intended use rather than assuming uniform performance.
help_terms_en: Clinically acceptable: Judged by reviewers as usable for planning with no edits or only minor edits.
clinical_context_en: Postoperative sites such as the prostate bed or post-mastectomy chest wall have altered anatomy and surgical clips, and usually make up a small part of any validation set.

question_en: A pulmonary-nodule classifier had 90% overall accuracy during validation and labels a new nodule as malignant. Which conclusion is justified by these facts alone?
option_1_en: The model's 90% accuracy means that nine in ten positive predictions were malignant.
option_2_en: A 90% accurate classifier is too unreliable for its positive labels to carry diagnostic information.
option_3_en: Because the model was validated, its positive label can be treated as confirming malignancy.
option_4_en: The label and overall accuracy alone cannot tell you this particular patient's probability of malignancy.
explanation_en: Overall accuracy is not positive predictive value or an individual probability. A positive label reflects the classifier's decision rule, often a threshold applied to a score, and it can still be informative. Interpreting risk requires relevant performance evidence such as positive predictive value in a comparable population, the score's meaning and calibration where applicable, and the clinical context.
help_terms_en: Classifier: A model that assigns each case to a category, such as benign or malignant.
clinical_context_en: AI nodule classifiers are used in lung screening and staging CT. Before lung SBRT, a 'malignant' label may influence decisions such as treating without a biopsy.

question_en: An AI tool reports 99% confidence on an unusual clinical case. Which statement best describes how this score should be interpreted?
option_1_en: The diagnosis is correct with a 99% probability.
option_2_en: The score indicates the models confidence in its prediction, but this is not related to its accuracy.
option_3_en: The high confidence score means the AI tool has been developed and validated for unusual cases.
option_4_en: The high confidence score suggests that the case falls within the models intended area of use.
explanation_en: A confidence score is not an individual guarantee of correctness. Its interpretation as a probability requires evidence of calibration in relevant cases, which may not extend to unusual inputs. Scores can still be informative, for example to rank or flag cases, but this use also needs evaluation and an appropriate clinical review process.
clinical_context_en: Some contouring, QA and decision-support tools display a confidence value or percentage with each output, and reviewers may use it to decide if the output is trustworthy.

question_en: A model reports aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Which distinction helps identify what additional information might reduce the uncertainty?
option_1_en: Epistemic uncertainty is reducible with more representative training data; aleatoric reflects ambiguity in the observations.
option_2_en: Aleatoric uncertainty is reducible with more representative training data; epistemic reflects ambiguity in the observations.
option_3_en: Aleatoric uncertainty reflects differences between hospitals; epistemic reflects disagreement between clinicians' contours.
option_4_en: Aleatoric uncertainty is the error on training patients; epistemic uncertainty is the error on validation patients.
explanation_en: Aleatoric uncertainty is relative to the available observations and task; better acquisition or additional information may reduce some ambiguity. Epistemic uncertainty may reduce with informative, representative training data and appropriate modelling. Disagreement between clinicians' reference contours contributes to aleatoric (label) uncertainty. The decomposition is model-dependent and requires evaluation; a total uncertainty score does not automatically separate these sources.
clinical_context_en: Some newer contouring tools display uncertainty maps that highlight where a boundary is less certain, intended to focus clinician review on those regions.

question_en: A model predicts each patientâs risk of developing pneumonitis within one year. In a local validation cohort of 200 patients, its ROC-AUC is 0.90 and the average predicted risk is 20%. However, 80 patients (40%) develop pneumonitis within one year. Which interpretation is correct?
option_1_en: Given the high ROC-AUC, a 20% risk threshold is likely to select the intended level of risk.
option_2_en: The model overestimates risk in this group, so its risk estimates should be adjusted downwards.
option_3_en: The model ranks patients well, but underestimates risk on average in this cohort.
option_4_en: The high ROC-AUC is unreliable, because a miscalibrated model cannot discriminate well.
explanation_en: ROC-AUC measures discrimination, whereas calibration concerns agreement between predicted risks and observed outcome rates; a model can discriminate well and still be miscalibrated. This example suggests underprediction in the stated group. Assess calibration with uncertainty intervals, particularly near decision thresholds. Clinical usefulness also depends on the benefits and harms of the proposed action, not calibration alone.
help_terms_en: ROC-AUC: Short for 'receiver operating characteristic, area under the curve'.
clinical_context_en: Pneumonitis risk models are used to individualise lung dose constraints and to counsel patients. A predicted risk is often compared with a threshold when choosing between plans.

topic: Prediction vs Causation in Outcome Models
question_en: A toxicity model was trained for prediction on observational data. A user changes one input to simulate a treatment modification and obtains a lower predicted risk. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
option_1_en: An input with a large contribution to the prediction is likely to be a worthwhile target for treatment.
option_2_en: A predictive association alone does not establish the effect of intervening on that variable for this patient.
option_3_en: The model is invalid, because observational data cannot support any clinical prediction.
option_4_en: The lower prediction gives a reasonable estimate of the reduction the treatment change would achieve.
explanation_en: Prediction from observational associations does not by itself identify intervention effects, although observational data can support valid prediction. Feature importance and simulated changes to inputs can be affected by confounding and relationships between variables. Supporting causal evidence and assumptions, or relevant intervention studies, are needed to justify a treatment-effect claim.
help_terms_en: Toxicity model: A model that estimates the risk of a treatment toxicity, such as xerostomia or pneumonitis, from clinical and dose information.
clinical_context_en: Some planning and decision-support tools let users adjust dose or treatment inputs and see the predicted toxicity risk update instantly.

question_en: An AI contouring tool is CE-marked or FDA-cleared/approved for its intended use and has published multicentre results. What is the most appropriate step before clinical introduction?
option_1_en: Confirm correct installation and that outputs match the vendor's results on vendor provided test data.
option_2_en: Demonstrate acceptable performance within the intended use on relevant local cases and workflows.
option_3_en: Repeat a multicentre validation of the same scale as the published study before any clinical use.
option_4_en: Rely on the published results, provided the model version and intended use match the purchase.
explanation_en: Regulatory status and published evidence inform evaluation but do not establish local performance, and installation checks are necessary but not sufficient. Local commissioning should assess relevant patients, inputs, workflows and predefined acceptance criteria, with scope proportionate to intended use and risk; repeating a study of multicentre scale is not required. CE marking and FDA clearance or approval are different regulatory routes.
help_terms_en: CE marking: Shows that a device meets EU regulatory requirements for its stated intended use. | FDA clearance or approval: US regulatory routes that allow a device to be marketed for its intended use. | Intended use: The purpose, patient group and setting the manufacturer specifies for a device.
clinical_context_en: Under the EU Medical Device Regulation, AI contouring and planning tools are medical devices, and many now carry CE marking or FDA clearance.

question_en: For testing model performace on local data, which dataset design is the most approprite?
option_1_en: Typical local cases only, sampled to exclude artefacts and postoperative anatomical changes.
option_2_en: A large public benchmark dataset, so that results can be compared with other centres.
option_3_en: Representative local cases plus a separately analysed set of relevant challenging cases.
option_4_en: Challenging local cases only, pooled to estimate performance during routine clinical practice.
explanation_en: Representative cases estimate routine performance, while a challenge set explores relevant failure modes. Analyse these appropriately rather than treating an enriched challenge set as routine prevalence. Public benchmarks aid comparison but do not reflect local protocols or populations. Use independent evaluation data and cover relevant local protocols, populations and annotation guidance.
help_terms_en: Public benchmark dataset: A shared, openly available dataset that different groups use to compare algorithms.
clinical_context_en: Choosing which local cases to test is one of the main decisions when commissioning an AI tool, and is often limited by the staff time needed to contour them.

question_en: You consult a model card to assess whether an AI contouring tool is appropriate for a particular patient and scan. Which information is most directly relevant?
option_1_en: Training and validation populations, intended use, input requirements and known limitations of the tool.
option_2_en: Network architecture, number of trainable parameters and graphics hardware used during model development.
option_3_en: Total training image count, publication count and the vendor's overall average performance score.
option_4_en: Software installation requirements, licensing arrangements and the model's average processing time per scan.
explanation_en: Intended use, development and validation populations, input constraints, subgroup results and known limitations help users assess applicability. Technical and operational details can matter for other purposes. Documentation informs the decision but does not establish that an individual output is correct.
help_terms_en: Model card: A standardised summary document supplied with an AI model.
clinical_context_en: Vendors increasingly supply model cards or similar product summaries alongside technical files and user manuals.

question_en: A vendor releases an updated version of an AI contouring model used in your clinic. Which approach is most appropriate before the update enters clinical use?
option_1_en: Review the changes and revalidate affected functions in proportion to the change and its risk.
option_2_en: Repeat user training and retain the existing validation because the intended use is unchanged.
option_3_en: Repeat the full original commissioning for every update, whatever the extent of the change.
option_4_en: Check processing speed and file compatibility, then monitor performance once routine use resumes.
explanation_en: Model changes can alter clinical behaviour, so existing validation cannot simply be retained. Review release notes, assess the change and revalidate proportionately against clinical acceptance criteria and prior performance; full recommissioning is not needed for every update. Update records and staff guidance, maintain a contingency plan including rollback where appropriate, and continue monitoring.
clinical_context_en: Cloud-hosted AI tools can be updated by vendors several times a year, with release notes ranging from detailed to very brief.

question_en: An audit identifies missed errors in approved AI contours. Which finding most strongly suggests that reviewers have become over-reliant on the AI?
option_1_en: Reviewers skip usual anatomical checks because previous AI contours have rarely needed correction.
option_2_en: Segmentation monitoring tools evaluating editing practice have not changed over time.
option_3_en: Reviewers miss subtle boundaries because image artefacts make the anatomy difficult to assess.
option_4_en: Reviewers shorten checks because interruptions leave insufficient time to complete their usual review.
explanation_en: Previous reliable performance can encourage reviewers to assume that subsequent outputs are also correct and reduce their checking. This is characteristic of automation-related complacency. Fewer edits, missed errors or shorter reviews alone do not establish over-reliance; the reason for the behaviour matters.
clinical_context_en: In many departments, oncologists and RTTs now edit and approve AI contours for most patients, often between other clinical tasks.

question_en: With the model version unchanged, the average number of contour edits per patient has decreased over time. Which additional finding would provide the strongest evidence that reviewers are becoming less vigilant and missing clinically important errors?
option_1_en: The proportion of contours accepted without modification has increased, while independent audit results show no change in clinically important error rates.
option_2_en: Reviewers spend less time on contours that consistently meet predefined clinical acceptability criteria.
option_3_en: An independent audit of comparable cases finds an increased rate of clinically important errors in contours approved without correction by reviewers.
option_4_en: The number of edits per patient has decreased primarily in anatomical regions where the model previously showed high agreement with expert contours.
explanation_en: Finding more important errors in accepted outputs is direct evidence of reduced review performance, although it does not prove automation bias. Shorter review times are consistent with over-trust but also with growing familiarity, so they are weaker evidence. Edit rates can also change with case mix, input protocols, reviewer preferences and experience. Interpret edit rates alongside independent quality audits, review conditions and version history.
help_terms_en: Edit rate: How much reviewers change AI contours before approving them, for example the number or size of edits per patient.
clinical_context_en: Edit rates are easy to log automatically, so departments often use them to monitor AI contouring tools after go-live.

question_en: An AI-assisted treatment plan is reviewed and approved by the clinical team. Which statement best describes professional accountability?
option_1_en: When an approved tool is used as intended, accountability for accepting its outputs rests with the manufacturer.
option_2_en: Each professional remains accountable for decisions within their role; other parties retain their own responsibilities.
option_3_en: Approving the plan makes the approving professional solely accountable for errors arising anywhere in the AI workflow.
option_4_en: Once the tool passes local commissioning, accountability for accepting its outputs transfers to the commissioning team.
explanation_en: Using an approved AI tool does not remove the responsibilities of the professionals who review and approve a plan for their decisions and appropriate use of the system. Professional accountability is not the same as sole legal liability: liability for a particular incident depends on the circumstances, and organisational and manufacturer responsibilities are separate considerations.
help_terms_en: AI-assisted plan: A treatment plan in which AI produced contours, dose or plan settings that staff then reviewed.
clinical_context_en: AI contours and plans now pass through several professional groups, including oncologists, physicists, dosimetrists and RTTs, and sign-off processes vary between departments.

question_en: A colleague pastes an identifiable oncology clinic letter into a public chatbot that the organisation has not approved for patient data. What is the main information-governance concern?
option_1_en: The main concern is the accuracy of the chatbot's output, which must be checked before use.
option_2_en: The disclosure is acceptable if the colleague deletes the conversation history straight afterwards.
option_3_en: Turning off the chatbot's model-training setting would make this an authorised use of patient data.
option_4_en: Identifiable patient data were disclosed to an unapproved service without an authorised arrangement.
explanation_en: The concern is unauthorised processing or disclosure, including how the service uses, retains and protects the data. Deleting the history or disabling training afterwards does not undo the disclosure or provide authorisation, and output accuracy is a separate concern. Approved systems may process identifiable data under appropriate arrangements; removing a name alone may not make a clinical narrative anonymous.
help_terms_en: Identifiable data: Information that could identify a patient directly, such as a name, or indirectly, such as a rare diagnosis combined with dates and hospital. | Public chatbot: A general-purpose AI assistant that anyone can use online.
clinical_context_en: Staff increasingly use general-purpose AI assistants to draft and summarise clinic letters, referral notes and patient information.

question_en: An AI-generated synthetic CT scan looks anatomically realistic, but the calculated radiation dose differs from that based on the reference CT near the nasal sinuses. What is the most likely explanation?
option_1_en: As the anatomy looks correct, the discrepancy most likely arises in plan optimisation, not the image.
option_2_en: Incorrect CT numbers at air-bone interfaces may give wrong density or material assignments.
option_3_en: The discrepancy reflects display windowing, since CT-number errors do not change calculated dose.
option_4_en: The reference CT is likely to be at fault, because the synthetic CT appears anatomically realistic.
explanation_en: Visual realism does not establish quantitative accuracy. Conventional MRI does not distinguish air from cortical bone well, so incorrect CT numbers near air-bone interfaces can lead to unsuitable density or material assignments for dose calculation. Evaluate physical and dosimetric accuracy using appropriate reference methods. This is the most plausible explanation to investigate; the scenario alone does not confirm the actual cause.
help_terms_en: Synthetic CT: A CT-like image generated from MRI so that dose can be calculated without a planning CT. | CT number: The value of each voxel in a CT image, measured in Hounsfield units.
clinical_context_en: MRI-only planning is used for prostate and increasingly for brain and head-and-neck sites, avoiding CT-MRI registration uncertainty.

topic: Predicted Dose and the Final Treatment Plan
question_en: An AI model predicts a three-dimensional dose distribution that meets target and organ-at-risk criteria. Which statement about using that prediction for treatment planning is most accurate?
option_1_en: Once its dose-volume histogram is reviewed, the predicted distribution can be used as the plan.
option_2_en: Dose predictions are too unreliable to guide planning and so should not be used as optimisation goals.
option_3_en: The final plan must be evaluated in its own right, as achievable doses often differ from predicted ones.
option_4_en: The final plan inherits the prediction's validation results if it is generated for the same patient.
explanation_en: A dose prediction is not necessarily a physically deliverable treatment plan, although it can be a useful optimisation goal or quality benchmark. Subsequent optimisation and delivery constraints can change the achieved distribution. Evaluate the final plan's target coverage, organ-at-risk doses, other clinical criteria and deliverability rather than assuming that prediction quality establishes plan quality.
help_terms_en: Dose prediction model: An AI model that estimates a 3D dose distribution for a patient from their images and contours. | DVH: Dose-volume histogram, a graph summarising the dose received by each structure.
clinical_context_en: Knowledge-based and AI dose-prediction tools are increasingly built into treatment planning systems.

topic: Clinical Use of Large Language Models
question_en: A large language model drafts a fluent clinical summary with patient details and guideline references. Which verification approach is most appropriate before clinical use?
option_1_en: Check the writing for internal consistency and accept details that occur repeatedly within the summary.
option_2_en: Check each patient-specific claim against the record and each cited guideline at source.
option_3_en: Ask the same model to confirm the accuracy of its draft and accept any details it reconfirms.
option_4_en: Check a random sample of details against the record, as checking every claim defeats the purpose.
explanation_en: Fluent text can contain unsupported patient details, incorrect recommendations or fabricated citations. Verify each patient-specific claim against the record and check cited sources, including whether references support the stated claim; spot-checking a sample can miss errors. Retrieval and other verification tools can help but do not guarantee accuracy.
help_terms_en: Large language model (LLM): An AI system trained on large amounts of text to generate written responses.
clinical_context_en: LLMs are being piloted to draft clinic letters, treatment summaries and discharge notes from patient notes.

question_en: A generative AI tool denoises a CBCT image and produces sharp, realistic anatomical detail. Which interpretation of the restored image is most appropriate?
option_1_en: Sharper boundaries show that the model has recovered the anatomy hidden by the noise.
option_2_en: Detail absent from the original image can be accepted if the restored image is internally consistent.
option_3_en: Denoised CBCT images should not be used clinically, even for tasks such as image matching.
option_4_en: It may add unsupported detail or remove real features while appearing anatomically realistic.
explanation_en: Learned image restoration uses measured inputs and learned prior information. It can introduce unsupported structures or remove real features while improving apparent image quality. Evaluation must address anatomical fidelity and the intended clinical task, not visual sharpness alone; restored images can be used for tasks for which they have been validated.
help_terms_en: CBCT: Cone-beam CT acquired on the treatment unit, mainly for patient positioning. It is noisier than planning CT. | Denoising: Processing that reduces image noise. | Image matching: Aligning the CBCT with the planning CT to correct patient position before treatment.
clinical_context_en: AI-enhanced CBCT images are being introduced for daily image guidance and online adaptive radiotherapy.
